summary: Defines the basic components of a Network Standard Data Specification syntax, a mechanism for specifying all the attributes of a collection of bits. It replaces RFC 615.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a way to describe exactly what a pile of data looks like, so any computer can understand it.

questions: describing data format on the arpanet
subtitle: A 1974 proposal for a common way to name a file on any network host, in forms for humans and for programs.

tldr.problem: Each host names files differently, so there was no common way to say exactly where a collection of bits lives on the network.
tldr.mechanism: A Network Standard Data Specification starts with % or %% and is a series of keyed fields such as HOST, DIR and FILE, in a human-friendly form or a fixed-format machine form.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the basic syntax and the pathname fields only, leaving other file attributes for later, and it replaces RFC 615.

today: This RFC replaces RFC 615. Its status is listed as Unknown, and the text says that the complete NSDS syntax was still to be defined.

sections.title: Goals and Two Modes
sections.content:
A Network Standard Data Specification (NSDS) is meant to specify all the attributes of a collection of bits. The full syntax needs extended effort, so this document gives only a basic syntactic environment plus a complete syntax for the pathname, meaning the information that specifies the location of the bits. It is essentially the pathname syntax of RFC 615, changed to allow other file attributes to be added and to suit both people and processes.

There are two modes. In semi-structured mode, for humans, keywords are variable length, may be abbreviated if still distinct, and data is surrounded by delimiter characters. In highly-structured mode, for computers, keywords are fixed length and each data subfield begins with a byte count.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a version for people, with brackets and short names, and a version for computers, with exact sizes.

sections.title: The Field Syntax
sections.content:
An NSDS begins with a flag of one percent sign (semi-structured) or two (highly-structured), then the fields, and ends with a space. Pathname fields come before any other attribute.

In the machine form each field is a 4-character keyword, a one-byte binary count and then the data. In the human form each field is a keyword followed by data between a left and right delimiter. The delimiter may be any non-alphabetic printable character not in the data, or a bracket pair. Case is irrelevant to the syntax, and pathname fields are order dependent, though defaulted ones may be omitted. Fields may repeat, so several DIR fields can describe nested directories.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of the address has a label and a value. People wrap the value in brackets, and computers say how many characters it has.

sections.title: Pathname Keys, Devices and Defaults
sections.content:
The pathname keys, in order, are NETWORK, HOST, PERIPHERAL, VOLUME ID, DIRECTORY, FILE, TYPE, VERSION and SITEPARM. The SITEPARM field carries a site-specific item such as an access specification or account number, and any attribute not yet defined must go there.

The RFC reserves peripheral names such as DISK (or DSK), ONLINE, TAPE, OFFLINE, LINE PRINTER and CARD READER. Defaults are guidelines: network ARPA, the host interpreting the NSDS, peripheral ONLINE (DISK), and the user's current working directory. For numbers in human-form fields, a trailing letter gives the radix, H for hexadecimal, O for octal, B for binary and D for decimal, with ten as the default.
sections.plainLanguage: The address pieces go in a fixed order, from network and computer down to folder and file name, and missing pieces are filled with sensible guesses.

sections.title: Sample Pathnames
sections.content:
The RFC shows the same file in both modes. A message file at ISI is written %H[ISI]D<DCROCKER>F(MESSAGE>T(TXT)S/P770404/ followed by a space in the semi-structured form. A file at UCLA-CCN uses several DIR fields, one for each directory level, and a Multics example starts with an empty directory value to mean the top of its directory structure.

The author notes that an earlier first version mixed Tenex and Multics conventions and was easier to type but lacked extensibility, so it was dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC writes out real file addresses both ways so you can see that they describe the same file.

items.desc: The host machine holding the bits.

items.label: Volume
items.desc: The tape reel or disk pack on that device.

items.desc: Directory pointing to the next entity named.

items.label: Type
items.desc: Optional modifier to the file name.

items.label: Site parameter
items.desc: A site-specific item such as an account number.
